Paths to consider

A path starts with one paper problem and leads to automation. These three already have a client story on your site.

Onboarding paperwork

Who it's for
HR and volunteer offices, mostly at school districts
The problem
Forms and attachments are scattered, links don't work, and someone has to chase every signature.
Forms to start with
New employee onboarding, Volunteer applications
Then automation
Approvals that route on their own, with every form saved to the right record.
What you already have
Two client stories already on your site: HR Onboarding of New Employees, and Volunteer Onboarding at a School District.

Time cards and payroll

Who it's for
Payroll and site offices, mostly at school districts
The problem
Paper time cards pile up, until hundreds of cards turn into thousands.
Forms to start with
Time cards, Mileage forms
Then automation
Supervisor approval in order, then hours handed to payroll without retyping.
What you already have
One client story on your site: Paper Time Cards. A district time card project is also underway.

Purchasing and payments

Who it's for
Finance and purchasing offices at counties, cities, and other public agencies
The problem
Purchase orders are handled by hand, and payments slip through the cracks.
Forms to start with
Purchase orders, Invoices
Then automation
Approvals routed by department, with a clear record of who approved what.
What you already have
One client story on your site: Purchase Orders, Invoices, and Payments.

Others worth a look

  • Incident reports for risk management
  • Public records requests
  • Replacing old Access databases

A sample sales plan

What a one-page plan could look like, using onboarding paperwork as the example.

Who to callHR and volunteer offices, mostly at school districts
First questionWhen someone new is hired, how many forms do they fill out, and where do those forms go?
Demo withNew employee onboarding
Story to tellTwo client stories already on your site: HR Onboarding of New Employees, and Volunteer Onboarding at a School District.

The steps

  1. Pick. Choose the customers on your list who have this problem. Start with people we already work with.
  2. Open. Ask the first question. Listen before talking about OneForm.
  3. Meet. Offer lunch with their team, or a visit to the booth.
  4. Show. Demo the starting form, using their own paper form if they'll share it.
  5. Start. Walk them through the onboarding roadmap and agree on a first step.
  6. Stay. Keep sending the project updates, then suggest their next path.

What we'd love your input on

  • Do these steps match how you sell today?
  • What would you want to count?
  • How much should the sales team see?

Onboarding roadmap

A draft of how a new OneForm client could get started, written the way a client would read it.

123456789101112
1. Discover
2. Build
3. Connect
4. Test and pilot
5. Launch and support
6. Your next path

Months, based on one large project. Smaller forms would move faster.

1. DiscoverWe learn how your process works today.
You get: a clear plan, with owners and dates.
2. BuildWe build your forms and approval steps.
You get: working forms you can try.
3. ConnectWe link OneForm to the systems you already use.
You get: your data flowing where it needs to go.
4. Test and pilotA small group tries it before everyone does.
You get: fixes, training, and a go-ahead to launch.
5. Launch and supportEveryone goes live, with us close by.
You get: hands-on help while everyone settles in.
6. Your next pathWe look at results and pick what's next.
You get: a plan for your next paper process.

What we'd love your input on

  • Does this match how your projects really run?
  • How should the timeline and hours change for a small form or a rush?
  • Is the product OneForm or 1Form? Both are in use.
